Asthma patients taking the diabetes and weight loss drug semaglutide may see a reduction in asthma attacks, a study suggests. The link between taking the drugs and asthma or COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) flare-ups was stronger among people taking higher doses of semaglutide.

And people with "more pronounced" asthma appeared to benefit more, researchers found. Semaglutide is the active ingredient in the weight loss drug Wegovy and the type 2 diabetes treatment Ozempic.

It is part of a group of drugs called GLP-1 receptor agonists, also known as GLP-1s, which help to lower blood sugar levels and slow down digestion, helping people stay fuller for longer.

"GLP-1 receptor agonists are widely used to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity. Previous research suggests that they may have anti-inflammatory effects and may improve lung-related outcomes, however, asthma and COPD outcomes have not been included as outcomes in GLP-1 drug trials," said study lead Professor Chloe Bloom, clinical associate professor in respiratory epidemiology at the National Heart and Lung Institute at Imperial College London.

"We wanted to use real-world health records to investigate whether people with asthma or COPD who started GLP-1 receptor agonists had fewer acute respiratory attacks."

The study, presented to the European Respiratory Society Congress in Barcelona, Spain, examined whether a number of treatments were linked to a reduction in exacerbations. Experts examined UK medical records of tens of thousands of people who started GLP-1s.

Prof Bloom said: "The effect was strongest with semaglutide, especially in people with asthma, where use of semaglutide appears to be associated with nearly 40% reduction in asthma attacks. Semaglutide also led to a 20% reduction in COPD flare-ups."

She added: "The findings from this study are encouraging, but they should not change treatment decisions on their own. People with asthma or COPD should not start GLP-1 receptor agonists specifically for their lung condition outside current prescribing guidance. While the findings suggest that some people taking GLP-1 receptor agonists may experience fewer respiratory attacks, this needs confirmation in clinical trials."

Dr Alexander Mathioudakis, chairman of the European Respiratory Society's Group on Airway Pharmacology and Treatment, said: "This is one of the largest real-world studies to investigate GLP-1 receptor agonists and airways disease, and one of the first to examine whether effects differ between individual GLP-1 receptor agonists.

"It highlights the need to consider metabolic health as part of respiratory care. It also supports the case for including respiratory outcomes, such as asthma attacks and COPD exacerbations, in future trials of metabolic therapies."

title: Asthma patients taking weight-loss medication see 'attacks reduction'

Semaglutide has been shown in animal experiments to improve health and extend lifespan. Provided by Getty Images Bank.

The active ingredient "semaglutide" in the popular anti-obesity drug "Wegovy" and the diabetes drug "Ozempic" has been found to extend lifespan in animal experiments. Long-term clinical studies will be needed to determine whether it also prolongs human lifespan.

A research team led by Danica Chen, a professor in the Department of Metabolic Biology, Nutritional Sciences, and Toxicology at the University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley), confirmed that a "glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) drug" improves health and extends lifespan in mice, and published their findings on the 2nd (local time) in the international journal Nature.

Semaglutide is a drug ingredient that mimics the action of GLP-1, a hormone secreted in the gut. By directly binding to GLP-1 receptors, it increases satiety, suppresses appetite, and helps control blood glucose, and is therefore used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes. Health benefits such as reduced risk of various diseases, including cardiovascular, kidney, and liver diseases, have also been reported. The biological basis for these effects, however, remains unclear.

When semaglutide is administered, caloric intake decreases. Calorie restriction is associated with improved health and extended lifespan. The research team conducted a study to determine whether calorie restriction is the reason behind the diverse health benefits observed with semaglutide treatment.

The researchers continuously administered semaglutide or saline (control group) to female mice 20 months of age (equivalent to 60-65 years in humans) until they died naturally. As a result, the median lifespan of the semaglutide-treated group was 834 days, 12.4% longer than the 742 days of the control group. Median lifespan refers to the age of the mice at the time when 50% of them are still alive.

After three months of semaglutide administration, the semaglutide group showed increased exploratory activity in new environments compared with the control group, and improvements in physical functions such as grip strength, gait, and exercise, as well as in cognitive functions such as spatial memory. Indicators associated with aging -- including genomic instability, chronic inflammation, cellular senescence, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired proteostasis, and aging-related stem cell dysfunction -- were reduced.

In the "dentate gyrus," a brain region responsible for memory and learning, the researchers also observed increased markers of neural stem cell activity and a rise in the formation of new neurons. They thereby obtained evidence suggesting that semaglutide may help ameliorate neurodegenerative diseases.

The research team stated, "The health benefits of semaglutide are related to the metabolic advantages of eating less, but we also observed reduced aging-related markers and enhanced neurogenesis that cannot be explained by calorie re
title: Semaglutide Extends Lifespan in Elderly Female Mice at UC Berkeley

Eli Lilly's "Mounjaro" has expanded its indication into the cardiovascular disease field. Provided by Getty Image Bank

"Mounjaro," a popular obesity and type 2 diabetes treatment from US-based Eli Lilly, has received additional approval in the United States as a therapy that reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases such as myocardial infarction and stroke. After Denmark's Novo Nordisk secured cardiovascular protection indications for "Ozempic" and "Wegovy," the competition between the two companies that are leading the global obesity drug market has now expanded into the cardiovascular field.

According to the pharmaceutical industry on the 31st, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on the 28th (local time) approved Mounjaro as a treatment that reduces the risk of cardiovascular events in adult patients with type 2 diabetes.

Mounjaro is a dual-acting GLP-1/GIP agent. When food is consumed, two hormones -- glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) -- are secreted and promote insulin secretion. GLP-1 also regulates appetite and satiety, producing a weight-loss effect.

This additional approval is based on the results of a large-scale Phase 3 clinical trial in which Mounjaro was randomly compared with the cardiovascular drug "Trulicity." The trial followed 13,299 adults with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease for four years, dividing them into a Mounjaro treatment group and a Trulicity treatment group.

In the clinical trial, 12.1% of patients in the Mounjaro group and 13% in the Trulicity group experienced death from cardiovascular causes, myocardial infarction, or stroke. This confirmed that Mounjaro further reduced the risk of cardiovascular events and death compared with an existing cardiovascular treatment.

Previously, in March 2024, Wegovy received approval for an indication to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, and stroke in overweight or obese adults with cardiovascular disease, based on the results of a large-scale clinical trial.

Ozempic, which uses the same active ingredient (semaglutide) as Wegovy and is prescribed as a type 2 diabetes treatment, obtained its indication earlier, in January 2020, for adult type 2 diabetes patients with cardiovascular disease.

With this expanded indication for Mounjaro, Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk -- already locked in global competition in the obesity treatment market -- have widened their battleground to the cardiovascular disease treatment arena. Competition between the two companies for prescribing dominance in clinical practice is expected to intensify further.
title: Eli Lilly's Mounjaro and Novo Nordisk's Wegovy expand rivalry into cardiovascular drugs
author: dongascience.com

Premier Ben Carroll has defended state-funded weight loss injections for convicted mushroom murderer Erin Patterson, as she waits to hear whether she will be granted a retrial.

Asked on Tuesday if he was comfortable with Patterson receiving the medication while serving three life sentences, the premier said the decision to prescribe the 51-year-old Ozempic was based on medical advice, and that healthcare was a matter for individual prisoners and medical experts.

Weight-loss medications became available for prisoners in Victoria following an inquest into the death of Indigenous prisoner Michael Suckling, who died from an enlarged heart in March 2021 after gaining 117 kilograms while in custody.

Patterson, who is appealing her convictions, was recently prescribed the injections, according to the Herald Sun, while serving her minimum sentence of 33 years at the maximum-security Dame Phyllis Frost Centre in Melbourne's west, where she could be held in solitary confinement for years to come due to the notoriety of her case.

"What I know taxpayers want to know is that when there's a coronial investigation into a death in prison, that a government takes it seriously, and when it comes to medical advice, I will let the experts provide that," Carroll said on Tuesday.

Ozempic is listed on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for people with type-2 diabetes and costs about $25 a month under the scheme.

Opposition police spokesman Brad Battin said the reasons behind prescribing Patterson the weight-loss drug should be made public, stating some prisoners were receiving the medication for cosmetic reasons.

"Every person who's inside the prison system, they also get an hour outside their cell every day. It's up to them what they do," Battin said.

"If Erin Patterson chooses not to do exercise, then we shouldn't be subsidising a cost for medication to keep her weight down."

A Department of Justice and Community Safety spokesperson said access to weight-loss drugs was permitted only when there was a clear medical need, such as for the prevention of type-2 diabetes.

"Access to prescribed weight loss medication was introduced in response to recommendations from the coroner following a death in custody linked to obesity," a statement read.

Patterson pleaded not guilty to murdering her former in-laws Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister, Heather Wilkinson, and attempting to murder Heather's husband, Ian Wilkinson, by serving them a beef Wellington laced with death cap mushrooms at her home in July 2023.

During the trial, the mother of two told a jury she had struggled with body image and eating issues throughout her life.

She recalled binge-eating nearly an entire cake, telling the court that before making herself vomit, "I had a piece of cake. And then another. And another."

Patterson also said she had been planning to undergo weight loss surgery after the lunch, and had made up a fake cancer diagnosis that would explain to her family any trips to ho
title: Premier defends Erin Patterson's taxpayer-funded weight loss jabs
author: The Sydney Morning Herald

content:
For those who've struggled for years with working off (and keeping off) the kilos, weight-loss drugs like Mounjaro and Wegovy can seem like miracles beamed down from on high.

That is - miracles up to a point. Hair loss is a real reported side effect for some users of GLP-1 drugs. And while the other side effects, like nausea and digestive issues, might be worth enduring, hair loss can feel a bit different. You don't want to jump down three trouser sizes but get Tony Soprano's hairline.

Hair loss is far from guaranteed, to be clear. Clinical trials by Novo Nordisk, maker of Wegovy, found that hair loss can affect up to one in 10 patients. A clinical study for Mounjaro, meanwhile, saw that hair loss occurred in up to 5.7 per cent of patients, compared to 0.9 per cent of those on the placebo. What explains it? Research is still in an early phase, but a commonly agreed-upon theory centres on the sheer speed of the weight loss these drugs can produce. Any kind of rapid weight loss - the aftermath of giving birth, say, or a serious illness - puts the body through physiological stress. This can lead to a condition called telogen effluvium, where hair follicles enter into the "telogen" (resting) phase of their growth cycle prematurely and end up shedding the hair itself.

In other words, it's down to the actual, beneficial effect of the drugs - that rapid weight-loss - rather than the drugs themselves, so there probably won't be any real difference in hair-loss side effects between GLP-1 drugs. What might make a difference is your dosage. "The greater the weight loss, the greater the physiological stress on the body," says Dr Mohit Sodhi, a medical researcher at the University of British Columbia, who recently published a study on the link between semaglutide (the non-branded name for Ozempic and Wegovy) and hair loss. And the greater that physiological stress, the "greater potential for hair loss".

How to stop hair thinning while on weight loss medication

But just because hair loss is a side effect of the actual process of losing weight doesn't mean you have to just cross your fingers and hope you're not in the unlucky 10 per cent. Rapid weight loss comes with other effects which can contribute to hair loss - and which you can tackle with straightforward lifestyle changes. For one thing, says Dr Bhavjit Kaur, an aesthetic medical practitioner at London's Tuhi Clinic, users are frequently under psychological stress too: about their changing body and lack of appetite; about other possible side effects like nausea; even the cost of the drug they're on. Managing that stress via meditation, sleeping properly and exercise, and trying not to take on additional stresses elsewhere, like at work, is crucial.

What are the best supplements for hair growth when losing weight?

A reduced appetite is, well, kind of the point of these drugs. But you should still keep an eye on your nutrition. "Patients have less food intake that can potentially cause nutrient defi
title: How to tackle GLP-1 hair loss

NewsNation -- Over the last seven years, GLP-1 medication use in children age 8 to 11 has increased by nearly 31,000%, according to a new NYU Langone Health study.

The FDA has not approved any GLP-1 medication for children under 12, but in drastic circumstances, doctors have prescribed it off-label.

Researchers analyzed health records for 3,520,531 children with obesity but without diabetes. The share of those children ages 8 to 11 who were prescribed a GLP-1 rose from 0.03% in 2019 to 9.3% in 2026 -- a 310-fold increase. Kids with obesity-related conditions, from high cholesterol to sleep apnea, were substantially more likely to be prescribed the drugs than those without.

Dr. Babak J. Orandi, the study's lead investigator and associate professor in the Departments of Surgery and Medicine at NYU Grossman School of Medicine, told the New York Post that despite the sharp rise, only 0.6% of the study's 3.5 million children ever received a GLP-1 prescription over the full study period.

"In context, this is a very small number," Orandi says. "Against that denominator, 20,282 GLP-1 children receiving prescriptions represents a tiny fraction of children eligible for treatment. While the number receiving treatment is very small, uptake is accelerating quickly."

Orandi says he is more concerned about the "underlying factors" driving obesity, which affects roughly 1 in 5 American children.

Overall, the study found that GLP-1s so far seem to be reserved "for those at greatest cardiometabolic risk." Socioeconomic status also plays a role, with upper-income children more likely to be prescribed. Orandi notes, "most who could benefit still aren't."
title: GLP-1 prescriptions for kids up more than 30,000% since 2019

Weight loss products have always been popular, and scammers are known to take advantage of popular products and trends. Recently, GLP-1 medications have become a popular treatment for weight loss, diabetes, and other medical needs, so the demand is high and the availability is limited. This provides a perfect opportunity for scammers to target consumers with fraudulent sales listings and products.

Consumers may receive texts, emails, or social media ads promoting a weight loss product, click the link they are sent, and find an online pharmacy or health product retailer is selling it at a discounted price - and sometimes with no prescription needed. What they don't realize is that this is a fake website set up and promoted by a scammer to look like a legitimate seller. If they make a purchase through this website, they may receive a fraudulent product or no product at all - and all their payment information will be sent directly to the scammer.

Consumers may be convinced to try a product if someone they trust appears to support it, so some scammers are using A.I.-powered deepfake technology to create convincing representations of celebrities and health influencers endorsing "their" weight loss products. But the real person being impersonated has no involvement with the product at all.

Some consumers have purchased products online that claim to be GLP-1 medications. These include injections, pills, nasal sprays, liquid drops, and even skin patches. But when the products arrived, they did not contain the medication that was advertised, were a different brand than what the consumer purchased, or came from unlicensed or fake pharmacies.

Some scammers offer fake GLP-1 prescriptions through "telehealth" appointments, but these "prescriptions" are not written by a real doctor and can only be used at their fake or unlicensed pharmacy. Real GLP-1 medications require a prescription, cannot be bought over the counter, and are only available through state-licensed pharmacies. Consumers with questions related to their health or wellness, or a new medication, should consult their primary healthcare provider. If a consumer believes a product or service they purchased was misrepresented to them, they can file a complaint with DATCP.
title: Protect Yourself When Buying Weight Loss Products Online - KFIZ News-Talk 1450 AM
author: KFIZ News-Talk 1450 AM

As demand for aesthetic services continues to rise, medical spas face growing scrutiny over patient safety, clinical oversight and regulatory compliance. In this episode of "Counsel That Cares," host Morgan Ribeiro speaks with healthcare attorneys Brett Elliott and Kimberly Rai, along with New U Women's Clinic & Aesthetics Founder and CEO Rachel Fidino, ARNP, DNP, about the rapid expansion of the medical spa industry and the legal and operational challenges accompanying that growth. Bringing both legal and clinical perspectives, the speakers examine how scope-of-practice laws, supervision requirements and enforcement trends are shaping the industry. They also highlight the importance of strong compliance programs, active clinical leadership and accountability in managing risk, protecting patients and supporting sustainable growth.

Listen to more episodes of Counsel That Cares.

Learn more about medical spa compliance.

Podcast Transcript

Morgan Ribeiro: Welcome to Counsel That Cares. This is Morgan Ribeiro, the host of the podcast and a director in the firm's healthcare practice. Today, we are diving into one of the fastest-growing and most closely watched segments of the healthcare and consumer wellness economy, and that is the medical spa industry. Over the last several years, med spas have experienced explosive growth fueled by increasing consumer demand for aesthetic services, advances in noninvasive procedures and significant investment from private equity firms, family offices and strategic healthcare investors. What was once a fragmented cottage industry has matured into a sophisticated market, attracting substantial capital and driving consolidation across the country. But with that growth has come increased scrutiny.

Med spa operators and investors are navigating a complex web of healthcare regulations, corporate practice of medicine laws, fee-splitting restrictions, supervision requirements, licensure and registration obligations, there's marketing and advertising rules, there's privacy concerns and, of course, the evolving federal and state enforcement efforts. And as transactions become larger and business models become more sophisticated, for those who are operators or investors, it's really important that they understand the regulatory landscape, which has become just as important to understand as the underlying economics of the business. On today's episode, we'll explore the key legal and compliance issues shaping the med spa sector, discuss how investors are evaluating regulatory risk, examine common operational pitfalls and offer practical guidance for owners and management teams seeking to build compliant and scalable businesses.

And joining me today are several professionals who are in the trenches when it comes to the operations and regulations impacting the sector. I'm thrilled to have Brett Elliott, a healthcare regulatory partner in Holland & Knight's Seattle office, Kim Rai, a healthcare regulatory and transactions par
title: Podcast - The Medical Spa Boom: Clinical Autonomy, Patient Safety And The Evolving Compliance Landscape

- Healthcare professionals reported gaps in training and confidence around GLP-1 drugs for obesity

- Professionals raised concerns about weight regain and reduced engagement with lifestyle support

- The findings highlight the need for structured training as GLP-1 treatment becomes more widely used

Injectable GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide are increasingly being used to treat obesity, but healthcare professionals supporting patients on these medicines may not feel adequately prepared to manage them.

A qualitative study of healthcare professionals in a UK specialist weight management service found that most participants wanted more training and did not feel confident in their current understanding of GLP-1 drugs.

The professionals also raised concerns about weight regain after stopping treatment, reduced engagement with lifestyle support and how their roles may change as these medicines become more widely used.

At the same time, they saw GLP-1 drugs as a useful treatment option for some patients, particularly when lifestyle support alone may not be enough.

What Did Healthcare Professionals Say About GLP-1 Drugs?

A study in Obesity Science & Practice explored how healthcare professionals viewed injectable GLP-1 drugs for obesity treatment.

The research was conducted in a specialist Tier 3 weight management service in England that was preparing to introduce these medicines but had not yet started prescribing them.

Researchers interviewed 11 healthcare professionals, including nutrition advisors and behavioral change advisors.

None had prescribing rights, and most said they had received little formal training on injectable GLP-1 drugs and wanted more education.

Who took part in the study?

Detail

Number

Total participants

11

6

Male participants

2

Interview length

34 to 62 minutes

The overall attitude toward GLP-1 drugs was positive. Professionals saw them as a useful tool that could give some patients greater confidence during weight loss and provide an option between lifestyle support and bariatric surgery.

At the same time, they wanted GLP-1 treatment to be combined with lifestyle and behavioral support rather than used as a standalone solution.

Why Do Professionals Feel Undertrained on These Drugs?

A common thread across the research is that many professionals have not received formal training on GLP-1 drugs.

In the study, participants said they had learned about these weight loss medications mostly through their patients, not through their employer or any structured course.

One participant said they simply had not had the time to do their own research on the topic.

Another study backs this up on a larger scale. It surveyed 100 healthcare professionals and interviewed 20 more. The findings showed real gaps in obesity education generally and specifically in newer treatment options.

Investing.com -- Sandoz Group AG (SIX:SDZ) on Tuesday said it aims to more than double revenue by 2035 through a major expansion of its biosimilar portfolio, targeting a core EBITDA margin above 30% as it seeks to capitalise on a wave of drug patent expirations.

The Swiss drugmaker, speaking at a Capital Markets Day in London, set a goal it calls Bio100: building a portfolio of more than 100 biosimilars by 2040, up from 13 today.

It said the portfolio would expand its coverage of medicines losing exclusivity to around 80% from 2035, compared with about 50% currently.

Both the 2035 revenue doubling target and the above-30% core EBITDA margin ambition exclude the impact of GLP-1.

For the nearer term, Sandoz introduced a new mid-term outlook for 2025 to 2030, targeting mid-to-high single-digit percentage growth in average annual net sales at constant currencies and a core EBITDA margin of 25% to 27% by 2030.

Those targets include GLP-1. The company separately reaffirmed its existing mid-term outlook through 2028.

"Our Bio100 ambitions are set to position biosimilars to become the majority of our sales, broadening access for patients while creating significant value for shareholders," chief executive Richard Saynor said.

He added that the company held "a leading biosimilar pipeline, a scalable, flexible and cost-competitive biosimilar development, manufacturing and supply network." Sandoz recorded net sales of $11.1 billion in 2025.
title: Sandoz sees biosimilar expansion driving revenue, margins through 2035 By Investing.com
author: Investing.com

content:
A single contract win rarely reshapes a pharma company's growth story overnight, but when that win hands you exclusive, decade-long access to 70% of a country's demand for a cancer drug, it's worth pausing to understand what just changed.

Biosimilars have become one of the more significant battlegrounds in global pharma as governments seek to reduce the cost of complex biologics without compromising patient access. Brazil has a public healthcare system that serves the vast majority of the population, and has turned to Productive Development Partnerships (PDPs) to bring just that kind of localised, low-cost manufacturing onshore. Biocon has a long history of a biosimilars pipeline and manufacturing scale, and is now directly entering that framework for one of the most expensive drug categories in oncology.

Shares of Biocon Ltd.were trading at Rs. 396.35, up 1.26 percent from previous close of Rs. 391.40. The stock opened at Rs. 392.15, reaching an intraday high of Rs. 399.90 and low of Rs. 392.15. The company currently has a market capitalization of Rs. 64,397 crores.

What's the News?

On September 8, 2026, Biocon Limited announced that it has signed a partnership agreement with Bahiafarma and Bionovis for the supply of Pertuzumab in Brazil, marking its entry into the country's 10-year Productive Development Partnership program for the HER2-positive breast cancer therapy. The consortium of the three companies received 100% allocation under the program, giving Biocon exclusive access to a segment of the market that currently has no local manufacturing base for the drug at all.

That allocation matters because of the scale it unlocks: the PDP framework gives the consortium exclusive access to Brazil's public healthcare market, which accounts for approximately 70% of the country's total demand for Pertuzumab. Under the arrangement, Biocon will receive milestone payments along with a share of revenues generated from the opportunity over the full 10-year period, while the product itself undergoes phased localisation within Brazil in the mid to long term.

Financial & Business Analysis

Looking at the quarterly results of Biocon Ltd., the company's consolidated revenue increased by 9.17 percent YoY, from Rs. 4,021.6 crore in Q1 FY26 to Rs. 4,390.5. crore in Q1 FY27, and decreased by 3.91 percent QoQ from Rs. 4,569.1 crore in Q4 FY26.

In Q1 FY27 Biocon Ltd., consolidated net profit increased by 53.36 percent YoY, reaching Rs. 136.8 crore compared to Rs. 89.2 crore during the same period last year. As compared to Q4 FY26, the net profit has decreased by 31.12 percent, from Rs. 198.6 crore.

The basic earnings per share increased by 234.62 percent and stood at Rs. 0.87 as against Rs. 0.26 recorded in the same quarter in the previous year, FY2026.

For Biocon, this deal fits squarely into a strategy the company has pursued for years using partnerships and technology transfer to enter public healthcare systems that would otherwise be difficult to access
